solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Refills tankard, after knocking back drink

indicators.note: knocking something back turns it over, so the word for the tankard is read backwards here

parts.note: a tankard is a pot for beer
to sup is to drink, a sip at a time

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a pint and orders refills for the tankard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking back' looks like more drinking, but it is the signal to turn the tankard word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural-noun synonym: refills of a glass or a tank are additional amounts poured in to bring it back to full.

clue.text: Great fritters? Not half, when served with rice

indicators.note: food served up is dished out in a new arrangement, so these letters are rearranged
taking not half of the word fritters leaves only its first half

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner rates fritters as great, though only half a portion comes with rice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' is also British slang for 'very much', which sits nicely beside 'Great'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something terrific is excellent or wonderful, just as great is used informally in praise.

clue.text: Choose a deep-sounding instrument

indicators.note: sounding tells us the phrase is to be heard, so its spoken form gives the entry

parts.note: choose means pick, and deep means low, giving 'pick a low'

explanation.surface: A player is asked to pick an instrument with a deep sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deep-sounding' reads as one adjective, but 'deep' belongs to the words said aloud and 'sounding' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a small flute pitched an octave higher, a woodwind instrument of the orchestra.

clue.text: Make one train, turning up after losing case

indicators.note: in a down entry turning up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards
losing its case means the word drops its outer letters, the casing around the middle

parts.note: a retinue is the train of attendants following a dignitary

explanation.surface: Someone loses a suitcase on a train and makes an effort to reunite with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing case' strips RETINUE to ETINU; 'turning up' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to join things together so that they form a single whole is to make one of them.

clue.text: Protesting vigorously, having to cook chicken wing with a Primus

indicators.note: to cook is to alter or fiddle, so these letters are rearranged
a wing is at the side, so here it picks the end letter of the word chicken

parts.note: taken as written; a Primus is a camping stove

explanation.surface: A camper is up in arms at having to cook a chicken wing on a little camping stove.
explanation.walkthrough: N (chicken's last letter) and A PRIMUS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: being angrily indignant or vehemently objecting, as if taking up weapons over a grievance.

clue.text: Sorry, daughter's left appointment book in prison

parts.note: penitent means sorry for wrongdoing

indicators.note: the daughter has left, so her letter is taken out of the word for the book

parts.note: a diary is a book of appointments

explanation.surface: An apologetic note says the daughter has left her appointment book in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym, chiefly American: a penitentiary is a state or federal jail for convicted criminals.

clue.text: Queen playing free, in/around Bristol

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the next piece
playing suggests the letters are being played about with, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
Bristols is rhyming slang (Bristol City = titty) for breasts, so a Bristol is a tit

explanation.surface: A queen playing for nothing in or near the city of Bristol.
explanation.walkthrough: Bristol here is not the city: in Cockney rhyming slang Bristol City rhymes with titty. The slash lets 'in' be fodder and 'around' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Nefertiti was the queen consort of the Egyptian pharaoh Akhenaten, famous for her painted bust.

clue.text: Massage out-of-work clergyman in bunk

parts.note: to massage is to rub

indicators.note: out of means the following item is removed from the clergyman's title

parts.note: a bishop is a senior clergyman
OP, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: A redundant priest is given a massage in his bunk bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out-of-work' reads as unemployed, but splits into a removal signal and the musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: bunk is slang for nonsense, as is rubbish, meaning talk with no truth or value.

clue.text: Group send explicit message to film star

parts.note: to sext is to send a sexually explicit text message
ET is the alien star of Spielberg's film

explanation.surface: A group of fans sends a racy message to a film star.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a sextet is a group of six, typically musicians performing together.

clue.text: Wind up again, with kick in the arm?

definitions.meaning: split as ..., to wind into loops a second time
the backward jolt of a firearm felt in the arm, arm being a weapon

explanation.surface: Something is wound up a second time, giving a kick to the arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arm' looks like the limb but is a firearm, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: coiling a spring once more, and the sudden backward kick a gun gives when fired.

clue.text: Tin originally used by very loud bishop — neat tobacco holder

parts.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin

indicators.note: originally points to the first letter of the next word

parts.note: ff, fortissimo, is the musical mark for very loud
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
neat is an old word for cattle, so an ox

explanation.surface: A tin first owned by a booming bishop turns out to be a tidy tobacco case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neat' looks like tidy but is the old word for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a small box for powdered tobacco that is sniffed rather than smoked.

clue.text: Fail utterly, as motions often do

definitions.meaning: to collapse completely and be wasted
motions are bowel movements, which are flushed away down the toilet

explanation.surface: Like many proposals put to a meeting, something fails completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'motions' suggests proposals at a meeting; the second sense is lavatorial.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a British idiom for failing completely, and literally what is flushed down the toilet bowl.

clue.text: Got right press journalist dismissed

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them
ED, an editor, is the usual crossword journalist
a batter dismissed in cricket is out

explanation.surface: The press got things right once a journalist was sacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: problems that are sorted out or resolved have been smoothed away like creases.

clue.text: Push up bra is enhancing contents

indicators.note: the contents of these words are letters held within them, running across the word gap

explanation.surface: An advert for a push-up bra that enhances what it holds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contents' cheekily hints at what a bra contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to lift or elevate something upwards is to push it up.

clue.text: No nighties worn with abandon, not having got it together with anyone

definitions.text: not having got it together with anyone

indicators.note: with abandon means wildly, so these letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone sleeping naked, alone, without having got together with anybody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got it together' hints at romance; the definition means independently, not via someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: holding a title or status independently, through one's own merits rather than through association with another person.

clue.text: Perhaps hand out mixture, yet not suitable for everyone

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of order, rearranged

parts.note: U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for all ages

explanation.surface: Handing out a mixture that is not fit for everyone, like an adults-only film.
explanation.walkthrough: MIXTURE and YET are rearranged with 'not' removing U, the British 'universal' film rating.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a hand is an extremity of the body, a limb's farthest part, like a foot.

clue.text: That little bit extra provided by McFadden, du Maurier etc

indicators.note: the letters are supplied by these names, running across them

explanation.surface: Novelists like McFadden and du Maurier provide that little bit extra for readers.
explanation.walkthrough: Freida McFadden and Daphne du Maurier are novelists; 'etc' just rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an addition, especially extra material appended at the end of a book or document.

clue.text: Like Schubert's 8th, only done right?

parts.note: Schubert's Eighth is his Unfinished Symphony; if only the right side is done, the other side is not complete

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads two ways: abandoned before completion, and the left side not finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: Schubert's Symphony No 8 is known as the Unfinished, abandoned after two movements.

clue.text: Briefly wish to have back-up staff cover

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter goes

parts.note: to envy is to wish for what someone else has

indicators.note: in a down entry back-up means read upwards, reversing the word

parts.note: a staff is a pole

explanation.surface: A brief wish for backup staff to provide cover at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back-up staff' looks like reserve workers; it is POLE reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to envelop something is to wrap it up or surround it completely.

clue.text: Around Barnet, this keeps the rain off

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hat for the London district of Barnet that keeps off the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough but is rhyming slang: Barnet Fair = hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a fine mesh worn around the hair (Barnet) to hold it in place.

clue.text: Hat and cape lost where darts are thrown

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cape on maps
L stands for lost in tables of match results
the oche is the line darts players stand behind

explanation.surface: A woman loses her hat and cape at the pub darts match.
explanation.walkthrough: The oche is the throwing line in darts, a British pub game.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a bell-shaped close-fitting women's hat, popular in the 1920s.

clue.text: Left first lover at end of the quay

parts.note: Eve, Adam's partner, was the first lover

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Someone left their first love standing at the end of the quay.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a levee is a landing place on a river, a pier or wharf where boats tie up.

clue.text: Killer of Beatle reportedly sighed audibly

indicators.note: reportedly tells us Beatle is heard as beetle, the car

parts.note: heard as beetle: Herbie is the Volkswagen Beetle of the Disney Love Bug films

indicators.note: audibly tells us the preceding word is to be heard, its sound giving the letters

parts.note: the word sighed is said aloud, sounding like side

explanation.surface: The killer of a Beatle was reported to have sighed audibly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beatle is not John Lennon: heard as 'Beetle' it is Herbie, the Disney Love Bug car; 'Herbie sighed' said aloud gives the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a weedkiller, a substance used to destroy unwanted plants.

clue.text: State what ex-gardener might have said?

indicators.note: what someone might have said points to the spoken phrase, heard rather than spelt

parts.note: someone who once gardened might say 'I'd a hoe', I had a hoe

explanation.surface: A puzzle over what a retired gardener might remark.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Pacific Northwest.

clue.text: Phone one poet briefly about who inspired them?

parts.note: to phone is to call
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: about suggests the letters are moved around
briefly means shortened, losing the final letter

parts.note: a poet, cut short to three letters

explanation.surface: Phoning a poet about whoever inspired them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges POE to OPE. 'them' are poets: Calliope was the Muse of epic poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: in Greek myth Calliope was the Muse of epic poetry, inspiring poets.

clue.text: Drunk put in prison, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a can is American slang for prison, so to be jailed; perhaps as it could also be sacked or tinned

explanation.surface: A drunk is locked up, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: slang for heavily intoxicated, and jailed, from the American slang 'the can' for prison.

clue.text: Touring in Egypt around start of my vacation

indicators.note: around means the rearranged letters wrap the next piece
touring means travelling round, so these letters are moved about
start of picks the first letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A holiday spent touring Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacation' looks like a holiday but means clearing out, as in vacating a room.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the act of vacating a place, clearing it out so that nothing remains.

clue.text: A mechanical seat

definitions.meaning: one of the rude mechanicals, the workmen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, the weaver who wears an ass's head
the part of the body one sits on

explanation.surface: A mechanical seat, like a powered chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mechanical' is a noun: the rude mechanicals are the amateur actors in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: Nick the weaver in Shakespeare's play, and the buttocks one sits on.
